newsitem.title: GERMANY: German officials say EMU needs sound footing.
newsitem.headline: German officials say EMU needs sound footing.

text.p: Top German officials on Monday expounded their view that European economic and monetary union (EMU) must be sound to succeed.
Finance minister Theo Waigel said it would be better to wait for a good result on the proposed European stability pact than to move too quickly and have an unfavourable result.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler, meanwhile, added his voice to the chorus of German policy makers warning nations against window-dressing finances to join Europe's currency union.
Waigel, at the launch party for the flotation of Deutsche Telekom, told journalists, "It would be better to wait for a good result, rather than going too quickly."
Waigel said it would be good if an agreement on the stability pact came before the end of the year, "but we are not under pressure."

The stability pact, proposed by Waigel about a year ago, is aimed at ensuring that nations establishing a single European currency adopt tough fiscal policies that lead to stability for the Euro, as the currency is to be known.
At a meeting of European finance ministers last week, Germany insisted on stiff fines for countries that fail to keep the lid on budget deficits after the start of currency union.
Germany's tough stance in Brussels has fuelled speculation that Bonn wants to delay any agreement on a stability pact until 1998 when it is clear who will join EMU.

The finance minister told a German magazine over the weekend that if a satisfactory agreement on the stability pact could not be agreed, negotiations would have to continue after the EU summit in Dublin in December.
Zeitler, stressing that time pressure to join the union in the next decade should be turned into pressure to improve quality, said so-called creative accounting would not be helpful for the union.

"The new currency needs trust and its base capital must be the credibility that stability will be maintained. Creative accounting and a loose interpretation of the criteria can only weaken the currency's acceptance among European citizens and markets," Zeitler said.
Zeitler, also the president of the state central bank in Bavaria, made his comments in an article to be published in the next edition of the magazine "Politische Studien".

Germany has been a vocal opponent of nations' last minute efforts to whip their finances into shape and pass the strict entry criteria to be among the first nations to enter the currency union in 1999.
The European currency union will not offer a short-term improvement in the labour market. But the common currency is a key component for long-term growth, Zeitler added.
